title: You can be Moses (Teshuvah 5:2)
hook: every person can become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam

segments.voice: Yesterday, the path of return: recognize, regret, confess, resolve. You named one thing to turn from. Is it still in view today? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

Two names sit side by side in a law book. One is Moses, who stood on the mountain and brought down the Torah. The other is Jeroboam, a king of Israel who set up golden calves and led people away. You might expect a writer to put them at opposite ends of the universe, born different, made of different stuff. Maimonides does something stranger. In the middle of his laws of return, he puts the two names in the same sentence, and he puts you between them. Either one, he says, is open to you. Today's word is the sentence.
screen: `MOSES ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `JEROBOAM AND THE CALVES.` → `AND YOU, BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: You can be Moses. It comes from the fifth chapter of the Laws of Repentance in the Mishneh Torah. Turn it four ways. First, the claim. Maimonides writes that permission is given to every human being. If a person wants to turn toward the good way and be righteous, they can. If they want to turn toward the bad way, they can. And then the line: every person can be righteous like Moses our teacher, or wicked like Jeroboam. Wise or foolish, merciful or cruel. Second, what he's pushing against. He names an idea he calls foolish: that God decrees at birth whether a person will be righteous or wicked. No, he says. Nobody forces a person, nobody decrees it, nobody drags them down either road. The person chooses. Third, why it sits here, in the laws of return. Yesterday's steps would make no sense otherwise. If your character were fixed at birth, regret would be pointless and resolve would be theater. Return only works if the road can actually change direction. He even calls this freedom a great principle, a pillar of the Torah and the commandments, and grounds it in Deuteronomy, where life and good, death and evil, are set before the people, and the call comes: "therefore choose life." Fourth, the hard part. He knows this raises a question. If God knows everything ahead of time, how can a person really choose? He doesn't wave it away. He says the answer is beyond human understanding, because God's knowing is not like ours, and he holds on to both. God knows, and you choose. Readers have argued about that answer. But the sentence about Moses stands either way. Nothing written at your birth closes the road.
screen: `EVERY PERSON CAN TURN EITHER WAY.` · `NOTHING DECREED AT BIRTH.` · `WITHOUT CHOICE, NO RETURN.` · `GOD KNOWS, AND YOU CHOOSE.` · then, large: `YOU CAN BE MOSES.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your shoulders drop. Notice the small choices already in this moment. Whether to keep sitting. Whether to follow a thought or let it go. Whether to breathe a little slower. Pick one, and make it on purpose. Then think ahead to today. Find one moment where you usually run on autopilot: the reply you always give, the scroll you always start. Decide now, freely, what you'll do there instead. Just one. If you pray, you can hold the words "therefore choose life" for a breath. The bell holds the time.
You can be Moses. Maimonides' teaching that every person is free to become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam, and nothing at birth decides it. Today's word.
Your line: you can be moses. Today, when the autopilot moment you picked arrives, stop for one breath and make the choice yourself. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Some Jews study the Mishneh Torah's Laws of Repentance, including chapter five on free choice, in the season before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, when return is the theme.

fork.setup: you're Maimonides. a student asks: if God already knows what I'll do, how am I free? what do you answer?
options: God's knowing is beyond us; God knows, and you choose.
fork.reveal: he refuses to give up either side. God's knowledge isn't like ours, he says, so we can't grasp how they fit, but both are true.

original.note: Hebrew: permission, authority. Maimonides says this 'permission' to choose is given to every human being.

trapdoor: what you thought: some people are just born good, and some aren't.
what it means: every person can become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam; nothing decrees it.
what a scholar hears: Hilchot Teshuvah 5:1–5, where free choice is called a pillar of the Torah, and the knowledge-and-choice question is left beyond human grasp.

notes: Hilchot Teshuvah 5:1–2 paraphrased: permission given to every person; righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam, wise or foolish, merciful or cruel; the 'fools' who say God decrees at birth. Please confirm.

5:3 calls free choice a great principle and pillar of Torah and commandments, citing Deuteronomy 30:15 ('see, I have set before thee'); the script quotes 30:19 'therefore choose life' instead as the familiar verse. Confirm this pairing is acceptable, and confirm the JPS 1917 wording.
5:5 (God's knowledge and human choice; beyond human understanding) summarized. 'Readers have argued about that answer ever since' alludes to the Raavad's gloss and later discussion; kept general.
Original: רְשׁוּת as Maimonides' word in 5:1 ('רשות לכל אדם נתונה'); please confirm vocalization and gloss.
Jeroboam described from 1 Kings 12 (golden calves); confirm.

Editor: the teach no longer says Maimonides points to 'therefore choose life' (he cites Deut 30:15); it now says he grounds the principle in that Deuteronomy passage, whose call is 30:19.
